entries.title: Geofence Warrants and the Fourth Amendment
entries.subtitle: A legal analysis of federal appellate disagreement over geofence warrant constitutionality and the Supreme Court's pending review in Chatrie v. United States.
entries.publisher: Congressional Research Service, Library of Congress
entries.abstract: This legal sidebar examines the constitutional implications of geofence warrants—investigative tools that identify smartphones present in a geographic area during a specified timeframe. The document analyzes two primary Fourth Amendment issues: whether geofence data collection constitutes a 'search' under the Fourth Amendment, and whether a warrant sufficiently protects such searches. It focuses on diverging 2024 federal appellate opinions and discusses the Supreme Court's January 2026 grant of certiorari in Chatrie v. United States, situating geofence warrant jurisprudence within broader technology privacy doctrine including the third-party doctrine and Carpenter v. United States.

entries.title: Housden v. Stoyton (1568)
entries.subtitle: Early English common law case establishing a cause of action for defamatory statements regarding plague in a plaintiff's residence.
entries.publisher: Baker and Milsom Sources of English Legal History: Private Law to 1750 (2nd edn)
entries.abstract: Housden v. Stoyton (1568) represents an early English common law decision permitting an action on the case based on allegedly defamatory words. The case involved a defendant's statement that the plaintiff had harbored plague in his house and buried plague victims in his garden. The Court of Common Pleas upheld the maintainability of the claim, marking a significant development in the recognition of defamation as a general cause of action in English courts during the sixteenth century.

entries.title: Force v. Facebook, Inc.
entries.subtitle: Section 230 Immunity Shields Facebook from Civil Antiterrorism Claims
entries.abstract: In this appellate decision, the DC Circuit upheld dismissal of civil antiterrorism claims brought by U.S. citizens against Facebook for allegedly facilitating Hamas terrorist attacks through the platform's hosting of terrorist-generated content. The court held that Section 230(c)(1) of the Communications Decency Act provides broad immunity to interactive computer service providers who do not develop third-party content. The decision further clarified that Section 230 immunity is not implicitly narrowed by the Anti-Terrorism Act's civil remedies provision and that applying immunity does not create impermissible extraterritorial effects. The court declined supplemental jurisdiction over foreign law claims.

entries.title: Doe No. 1 v. Backpage.com, LLC
entries.subtitle: A First Circuit case examining claims against Backpage.com for alleged facilitation of sex trafficking of minors.
entries.abstract: This case involved minors who alleged they were trafficked through advertisements posted on Backpage.com. The plaintiffs brought suit alleging that Backpage tailored its website to facilitate sex traffickers' efforts to advertise victims, claiming violations of the Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization Act, Massachusetts General Laws chapter 93A, and intellectual property rights. The district court dismissed the action for failure to state a claim, and the First Circuit affirmed, finding that the allegations did not plausibly entitle plaintiffs to relief.

entries.title: Stratton Oakmont v. Prodigy
entries.subtitle: A landmark 1995 defamation case establishing internet service provider liability for third-party content on moderated forums.
entries.abstract: This case examined whether Prodigy Services Company should be held liable as a publisher for defamatory statements posted by anonymous users on its Money Talk bulletin board regarding Stratton Oakmont, Inc. and its president Daniel Porush. The New York State Supreme Court ruled that Prodigy's exercise of editorial control through content guidelines, automated filtering, and Board Leader moderators constituted publisher-level responsibility, distinguishing it from the earlier CompuServe decision. The case was settled in October 1995, but Congress subsequently enacted Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act of 1996 explicitly to overturn this precedent and provide broad immunity to internet service providers.

entries.title: Cubby v. CompuServe
entries.subtitle: A landmark internet case establishing that internet service providers function as distributors rather than publishers of third-party content.
entries.abstract: This case involved a defamation suit brought by Cubby, Inc. and Robert G. Blanchard against CompuServe and Don Fitzpatrick over allegedly false and disparaging remarks published in the newsletter "Rumorville." The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York dismissed all claims against CompuServe, ruling that the ISP lacked publisher liability because it exercised no editorial control over the content and had no knowledge of or opportunity to review publications before they became available to subscribers. The court likened CompuServe's role to that of a public library or newsstand. Though later complicated by Stratton Oakmont v. Prodigy, this decision established important precedent that was subsequently codified in Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act.

entries.title: Mark Foster et al. v. Richard H. Churchill, Jr., et al.
entries.subtitle: New York Court of Appeals decision examining tortious interference and defamation claims arising from the termination of co-CEOs by venture capital investors.
entries.publisher: New York Court of Appeals/ Cornell Legal Information Institute
entries.abstract: This 1996 New York Court of Appeals case addresses whether venture capital defendants Churchill and Croll tortiously interfered with appellants Foster and Franco's employment contracts with Microband Companies, a wireless cable television business. The court examined whether the defendants' role in terminating the appellants "for cause" and preventing severance payments constituted tortious interference and defamation. The decision considers the legal boundaries between legitimate business decisions by majority shareholders and wrongful interference with contractual relations, particularly in the context of employment termination disputes.

entries.title: Section 230: A Juridical History
entries.subtitle: An examination of Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act, its judicial interpretation, and implications for future internet law reform.
entries.abstract: This article provides a comprehensive analysis of Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act of 1996, which grants online entities immunity from liability for third-party content. While acknowledging the law's historical importance to internet development, the piece critiques its insufficient adaptability to technological change and examines the lower court interpretive decisions that constructed current immunity doctrine. The article serves as a guidebook for lawmakers and scholars by analyzing how interpretive missteps occurred, rather than proposing specific reforms, with the aim of informing more resilient immunity frameworks.

entries.title: Enigma Software Group USA, LLC v. Malwarebytes, Inc.
entries.subtitle: Analysis of how courts apply First Amendment doctrine to cybersecurity filtering determinations in the context of Enigma Software Group v. Malwarebytes.
entries.abstract: This legal analysis examines the Ninth Circuit's decision in Enigma Software Group v. Malwarebytes, which addresses whether cybersecurity companies' product classification determinations constitute protected speech under the First Amendment or actionable false advertising under the Lanham Act. The case raises fundamental questions about how existing commercial speech doctrine applies to technology platforms, specifically whether designations of software as malware constitute statements of opinion or verifiable fact. The court held that in the cybersecurity context, malware determinations are factual assertions due to the objective nature of the classification and the company's expertise, complicating liability assessments for cybersecurity firms.

entries.title: Gonzalez v. Google LLC
entries.subtitle: Supreme Court case analyzing whether online platforms can be held liable for algorithmically recommending harmful third-party content and the scope of Section 230 immunity.
entries.abstract: Gonzalez v. Google LLC addresses whether online platforms such as YouTube qualify for immunity under Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act when they use algorithms to recommend third-party content, specifically ISIS-related videos. The case arose from a 2015 terrorist attack in Paris that killed Nohemi Gonzalez, whose father subsequently sued Google for secondary liability under the Antiterrorism Act. The central legal question concerns whether Section 230 immunity extends to targeted algorithmic recommendations or only to traditional editorial functions such as displaying or removing content.

entries.title: Twitter, Inc. v. Taamneh
entries.subtitle: Analysis of how the Supreme Court's decision in Taamneh v. Twitter avoided establishing precedent on Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act despite significant opportunity to clarify internet service provider liability.
entries.abstract: This legal analysis examines the Supreme Court's handling of two consolidated cases (Taamneh v. Twitter and Gonzalez v. Google) concerning social media platforms' liability under terrorism statutes. The piece critiques the Court's decision to resolve the cases on narrow grounds while avoiding substantive interpretation of Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act, despite granting certiorari on this contentious issue. The author argues that this approach constitutes 'judicial ventriloquism' that fails to fulfill the judicial duty to clarify the law while simultaneously amplifying uncertainties regarding internet service provider liability under the Antiterrorism Act and the Justice Against Sponsors of Terrorism Act.

entries.abstract: On March 4, 2026, Nippon Life Insurance Company filed suit against OpenAI entities in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Illinois, alleging that an insured employee's use of ChatGPT for pro se litigation resulted in tortious interference with contract, abuse of process, and unlicensed legal practice. The case examines the generation of 44+ court filings, including fabricated case citations, allegedly produced by ChatGPT in response to the claimant's prompts following dissatisfaction with a prior settlement. This analysis discusses the factual background, three causes of action, relief sought ($10.3 million total), and evidentiary implications for AI liability and legal practice regulation.

entries.title: Moody v. NetChoice and NetChoice v. Paxton: A Narrow Path to Platform First Amendment Protections
entries.subtitle: The Supreme Court narrowly constrains First Amendment protections for social media platforms to guideline-based content moderation while leaving other curation practices subject to regulation.
entries.abstract: This analysis examines the Supreme Court's landmark decision in Moody v. NetChoice and NetChoice v. Paxton, which addressed the scope of First Amendment protections for online platform curation practices. The Court adopted a narrow approach, holding that only content moderation based on a platform's community and content guidelines constitutes clearly protected expression, while signaling skepticism toward broader protections for algorithmic curation and non-content-based ranking practices. The decision leaves substantial room for legislative regulation of platform design activities and rejects the technology industry's request for expansive First Amendment safeguards.

entries.title: Zeran v. America Online, Inc. (4th Cir.) (1997)
entries.subtitle: Analysis of the Fourth Circuit's foundational interpretation of Communications Decency Act Section 230 and its protection of ISPs from defamation liability.
entries.publisher: Free Speech Center at Middle Tennessee State University
entries.abstract: This case study examines Zeran v. America Online, Inc., 129 F.3d 327 (4th Cir. 1997), a seminal decision establishing broad immunity for internet service providers under Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act of 1996. The Fourth Circuit held that ISPs cannot be treated as publishers of third-party defamatory content and affirmed that Congress intended to prioritize free speech protection over liability for user-generated posts. The decision has become foundational precedent for online libel jurisprudence, with numerous federal courts adopting its interpretive framework in subsequent cases.

entries.abstract: This analysis examines the Ninth Circuit's May 2009 decision in Barnes v. Yahoo!, Inc., which clarifies the scope of Section 230(c)(1) immunity for internet service providers. The court upheld ISP immunity from negligence liability for third-party tortious content but held that Section 230 does not protect ISPs from promissory estoppel claims when they make explicit promises to remove harmful material and subsequently breach those promises. The decision raises important questions about incentives for ISPs to voluntarily moderate content and the appropriate balance between platform immunity and accountability.

entries.title: Fair Housing Council of San Fernando Valley v. Roommates.com
entries.subtitle: Ninth Circuit en banc decision establishing that CDA § 230 immunity does not apply when websites affirmatively require users to provide discriminatory information through pre-populated answers.
entries.abstract: In this precedential en banc decision, the Ninth Circuit held that Roommates.com could not claim immunity under the Communications Decency Act § 230 for requiring users to answer questions with pre-populated choices regarding protected characteristics (sex, sexual orientation, family status) in violation of the Fair Housing Act. The court distinguished between neutral tools that preserve CDA immunity and affirmative conduct that induces illegal expression, finding that mandatory discriminatory preference questions made the website a co-developer of unlawful content rather than a passive intermediary.

entries.title: The New York Times's About-Face: Copyright, Romantic Authorship, and the Generative AI Debate
entries.abstract: This legal analysis examines the New York Times's copyright infringement suit against OpenAI and Microsoft regarding the unauthorized use of Times articles in training large language models. The piece contrasts the Times's current invocation of romantic authorship theory and author protections with its opposing stance in New York Times Co. v. Tasini (1997), where the publisher prioritized its own financial interests over freelance authors' copyrights. The analysis reveals an apparent inconsistency in the Times's copyright positions and explores the broader tensions between protecting intellectual property and facilitating technological development.

entries.title: Transformative training: an analysis of AI training data and fair use in Authors Guild v. OpenAI Inc.
entries.subtitle: A technical and legal analysis of how copyright law applies to AI training on copyrighted materials.
entries.abstract: This paper examines the landmark case Authors Guild v. OpenAI Inc., which explores whether the use of copyrighted material in training datasets for generative AI constitutes copyright infringement or qualifies as fair use. Through technical analysis of GPT model architecture and training processes, the authors argue that AI training could be considered transformative use. However, ChatGPT's capacity to reproduce verbatim excerpts from training data complicates this argument and creates legal uncertainty. The court's decision will clarify how transformative use doctrine applies to artificial intelligence and likely establish precedent for future disputes.

entries.title: Getty Images (US) Inc (and others) v Stability AI Limited.
entries.abstract: This commentary examines the High Court judgment in Getty Images v Stability AI Limited, decided 4 November 2025, concerning copyright and trademark infringement claims arising from the training and deployment of the Stable Diffusion generative AI model. Despite initial expectations for comprehensive judicial guidance on AI and intellectual property law, Getty's claims were substantially narrowed during proceedings, resulting in limited findings of trademark infringement but no ruling on primary copyright claims and rejection of secondary infringement and damages claims. The judgment provides incremental clarification on model weights as articles, exclusive licensee requirements, and the scope of trademark infringement in AI-generated outputs, while leaving significant legal uncertainty in the field unresolved.

entries.publisher: U.S. Department of Justice, Office of Public Affairs
entries.abstract: On May 23, 2024, the Justice Department and 30 state and district attorneys general filed a civil antitrust action against Live Nation-Ticketmaster for alleged violations of Section 2 of the Sherman Act. The complaint alleges that Live Nation-Ticketmaster maintains unlawful monopolies in concert promotions and primary ticketing markets through exclusionary conduct including retaliatory threats against competitors, exclusive venue contracts, and exploitation of relationships with potential competitors. The lawsuit seeks structural relief and aims to restore competition, lower prices for consumers, and increase opportunities for artists and independent promoters.

entries.title: AI and Privilege After United States v. Heppner
entries.subtitle: Analysis of Judge Rakoff's ruling in United States v. Heppner regarding AI tool use and legal privilege protections.
entries.abstract: This analysis examines Judge Jed Rakoff's February 2024 decision in United States v. Heppner, which held that documents created by a criminal defendant using Claude are not protected by attorney-client privilege or work product doctrine. While the court's conclusion is legally sound, the opinion extends beyond necessary grounds by relying on a company's terms of service to find waiver of confidentiality. The analysis demonstrates that existing legal frameworks adequately address AI tool use in legal contexts without requiring novel doctrinal developments, and discusses implications for attorney-client relationships and the accessibility of AI-assisted legal services.

entries.title: United States v. Google, LLC
entries.subtitle: An analysis of the District Court's application of a lenient causation standard in finding Google liable for maintaining monopoly power through exclusive distribution agreements.
entries.abstract: This legal analysis examines the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia's landmark decision in United States v. Google, LLC, which found Google liable under Section 2 of the Sherman Act for maintaining monopoly power in general search services and search text advertising markets through exclusive distribution agreements. The court applied the Microsoft causation standard, permitting inference of anticompetitive effects without requiring but-for evidence, and determined that Google's agreements foreclosed 45-50% of relevant markets. The decision clarifies ambiguity surrounding causation standards in antitrust law while expanding enforcement agencies' ability to challenge allegedly anticompetitive conduct by large technology companies.

entries.title: United States v. Microsoft Corp.
entries.subtitle: An analysis of the landmark antitrust case against Microsoft and its implications for technology market regulation.
entries.abstract: This legal analysis examines the United States v. Microsoft Corp. antitrust case as a foundational litigation addressing competition policy in information markets characterized by economies of scale and network effects. The paper summarizes the factual and legal issues in the case, addresses the challenges of litigating complex antitrust matters in rapidly evolving technology sectors, and discusses the appropriate scope of antitrust enforcement in digital economies. As the first major case of its kind to be fully litigated, the analysis suggests this litigation will substantially shape the nation's antitrust policy framework for information technology markets.

entries.title: Amazon's Dominance and the Need for Antitrust Reform
entries.subtitle: A critical analysis of how Amazon's integrated business model and below-cost pricing strategy escape antitrust scrutiny under current consumer welfare doctrine.
entries.abstract: This legal analysis examines Amazon's multi-sector dominance across retail, logistics, cloud computing, and digital platforms, arguing that the company's predatory pricing and cross-business integration pose significant anticompetitive risks. The author contends that current antitrust doctrine, which prioritizes short-term consumer welfare measured through price and output, is inadequate to address market power in platform-based digital economies. The Note identifies specific vulnerabilities in existing antitrust frameworks and proposes two alternative regulatory regimes: restoration of traditional competition principles or application of common carrier obligations.

entries.title: In NetChoice Cases, Supreme Court Labels a Surprisingly Narrow Class of Online Platform Company Activities as Protected Expression
entries.subtitle: Analysis of the Supreme Court's landmark decision on First Amendment protections for social media platform content curation practices.
entries.abstract: This article examines the Supreme Court's combined decision in Moody v. NetChoice and NetChoice v. Paxton, which addressed the scope of First Amendment protections for online platform companies' content curation activities. The Court adopted a narrow interpretation, recognizing protected expression primarily in enforcement of platforms' content and community guidelines while signaling skepticism toward broader protections for algorithm-driven or non-content-based curatorial practices. The decision provides guidance that platform curation activities must be evaluated granularly rather than categorically, leaving substantial room for legislative regulation of platform design and content-agnostic practices.

entries.title: Section 230 and Child Exploitation: Restoring the Original Intent of the Communications Decency Act
entries.subtitle: A critical analysis of how Section 230 has been distorted from its original child protection purpose to provide near-absolute immunity to tech platforms.
entries.publisher: Mary Graw Leary / Villanova Law Review
entries.abstract: This article examines Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act, arguing that the statute was originally intended to protect children from exploitation online rather than to provide broad platform immunity. Through legislative history analysis and review of contemporaneous media coverage from 1996, the author demonstrates a significant gap between Section 230's original purposes and current internet realities, particularly regarding Child Sexual Abuse Material (CSAM). The article proposes reforms to restore Section 230 to its original intent while addressing contemporary digital harms.
